claim: The mouse olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) repertoire is composed of 10 million cells.
source: The mouse olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) repertoire is composed of 10 million cells and each expresses one olfactory receptor (OR) gene from a pool of over 1000.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kawagishi et al., 2014 in the Introduction section.

claim: Each OSN expresses one olfactory receptor (OR) gene from a pool of over 1000.
source: The mouse olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) repertoire is composed of 10 million cells and each expresses one olfactory receptor (OR) gene from a pool of over 1000.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations in the Introduction including Buck and Axel, 1991; Zhao et al., 1998; Hanchate et al., 2015; Saraiva et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2015; Chess et al., 1994.

claim: The OSN subtype distribution is stereotyped in genetically identical mice.
source: We find that the OSN subtype distribution is stereotyped in genetically identical mice, but varies extensively between different strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing high correlation (median rho = 0.89) between biological replicates of the same strain, as shown in Figure 1A and Figure 2A-B.

claim: The OSN subtype distribution varies extensively between different strains.
source: We find that the OSN subtype distribution is stereotyped in genetically identical mice, but varies extensively between different strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing 37% of OR genes are differentially expressed between B6 and 129 strains, and 50.8% between B6 and CAST strains, as shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Cis-acting genetic variation is the greatest component influencing OSN composition.
source: Further, we identify cis-acting genetic variation as the greatest component influencing OSN composition and demonstrate independence from OR function.
evidence: This claim is supported by F1 hybrid analysis showing concordance correlation coefficient of 0.86 between parental and allelic expression ratios, as shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: OSN composition is independent from OR function.
source: Further, we identify cis-acting genetic variation as the greatest component influencing OSN composition and demonstrate independence from OR function.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including analysis of newborn pups (Figure 4A), pseudogenes (Figure 4B), identical OR coding sequences between strains, and the Olfr2>Olfr1507 swap experiment (Figure 4C-E).

claim: Olfactory stimulation with particular odorants results in modulation of dozens of OSN subtypes in a subtle but reproducible, specific and time-dependent manner.
source: However, we show that olfactory stimulation with particular odorants results in modulation of dozens of OSN subtypes in a subtle but reproducible, specific and time-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing 36 OR genes significantly differentially expressed after 24 weeks of acute odor exposure (Figure 5B), with temporal dynamics shown in Figure 5C.

claim: OR gene mRNA level estimates in adult WOM increase, on average, 2.3-fold when using extended OR transcripts compared to Ensembl gene models.
source: With these models, OR gene mRNA level estimates in adult WOM increase, on average, 2.3-fold, but some increase almost 20-fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct comparison of expression levels using different gene models, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: OR mRNA expression values show high correlation between biological replicates with median rho = 0.89.
source: Nevertheless, they show a dynamic range of abundance levels (Figure 1A, inset) that are consistent between biological replicates, as indicated by their very high correlation values (median rho = 0.89, p<2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of biological replicates from RNAseq data.

claim: From the 94 OR genes of the Olfr7 cluster that have been deleted, 83 (88.3%) have no counts in any of the three biological replicates.
source: From the 94 OR genes of the cluster that have been deleted, 83 (88.3%) have no counts in any of the three biological replicates.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data from Olfr7 cluster deletion mice compared to controls, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There is very strong correlation (rho = 0.98, p=5 × 10−5) between OSN number determined by in situ hybridization and RNAseq expression value.
source: We find very strong correlation between OSN number and RNAseq expression value (rho = 0.98, p=5 × 10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ISH cell counts and RNAseq data for nine OR genes, as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is a strong selection bias towards OSNs that express OR genes with high RNAseq levels in WOM when collecting single OSNs (hypergeometric test, p=6.44 × 10−9).
source: Indeed, we find a strong selection bias towards OSNs that express OR genes with high RNAseq levels in WOM (hypergeometric test, p=6.44 × 10−9; Figure 1E), suggesting those OSN types are more numerous in the olfactory epithelium.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNAseq data from 63 randomly collected OSNs, as shown in Figure 1E.

claim: OR mRNA levels in single OSNs do not correlate with expression levels across the WOM (rho = −0.04, p=0.7518).
source: We find OR mRNA levels vary within the single cells, but this does not correlate with expression levels across the WOM (rho = −0.04, p=0.7518) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of OR mRNA levels in 63 single OSNs to WOM expression levels, as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Only 1.2% of the OR gene repertoire is significantly differentially expressed between B6 male and female mice.
source: By applying full gene models to these data, here we confirm their OSN distribution profiles are remarkably similar (Figure 2A); only 1.2% of the OR gene repertoire is significantly differentially expressed (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from B6 males and females, as shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The 129 genome has 4.4 million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 0.81 million small indels compared to B6.
source: The 129 genome has 4.4 million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 0.81 million small indels compared to B6 (Keane et al., 2011), of which we find 13,484 SNPs and 1,936 indels within our extended OR gene transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Keane et al., 2011 and analysis of the Mouse Genomes Project data.

claim: 13,484 SNPs and 1,936 indels are found within extended OR gene transcripts between 129 and B6.
source: The 129 genome has 4.4 million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 0.81 million small indels compared to B6 (Keane et al., 2011), of which we find 13,484 SNPs and 1,936 indels within our extended OR gene transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of genomic sequence data.

claim: 462 OR genes are significantly differentially expressed between 129 and B6 (FDR < 5%), representing 37% of the whole repertoire.
source: From the 1,249 OR genes, we find 462 are significantly differentially expressed (DE) compared to B6 (false discovery rate (FDR) < 5%), representing 37% of the whole repertoire (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from 129 and B6 strains, as shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: CAST strain has more than 17.6 million SNPs and 2.7 million indels relative to B6.
source: This strain has more than 17.6 million SNPs and 2.7 million indels relative to B6 (Keane et al., 2011); of these, we counted that 45,688 SNPs and 6,303 indels are found within our extended OR transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Keane et al., 2011 and analysis of the Mouse Genomes Project data.

claim: 45,688 SNPs and 6,303 indels are found within extended OR transcripts between CAST and B6.
source: This strain has more than 17.6 million SNPs and 2.7 million indels relative to B6 (Keane et al., 2011); of these, we counted that 45,688 SNPs and 6,303 indels are found within our extended OR transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of genomic sequence data.

claim: 634 OR genes are significantly differentially expressed (FDR < 5%) between CAST and B6, constituting 50.8% of the whole OR repertoire.
source: After mapping to a pseudo-CAST genome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), 634 OR genes are significantly differentially expressed (FDR < 5%) compared to B6, constituting 50.8% of the whole OR repertoire (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from CAST and B6 strains, as shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: 132 OR genes have differences of at least eight fold between CAST and B6.
source: The changes in expression for some OR genes are dramatic: 132 genes have differences of at least eight fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of differential expression data between CAST and B6 strains.

claim: 821 OR genes (65.7%) are differentially expressed between at least two strains (B6, 129, CAST).
source: Taking all pairwise comparisons into account (including 129 vs CAST, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E), 821 OR genes (65.7%) are DE between at least two strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by combined analysis of all pairwise strain comparisons, as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 136 OR genes are differentially expressed in all three pairwise comparisons (B6 vs 129, B6 vs CAST, 129 vs CAST).
source: One hundred and thirty-six of these are DE in all three pairwise comparisons (Figure 2G); for example, there are consistently different numbers of Olfr6-expressing OSNs in each strain (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of differentially expressed OR genes across all strain comparisons, as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There is a high correlation (rho = 0.98, p=5 × 10−5) between the difference in OSN number and the difference in RNAseq expression values between B6 and 129.
source: We find a high correlation between the difference in OSN number and the difference in RNAseq expression values between B6 and 129 (rho = 0.98, p=5 × 10−5; Figure 2K), demonstrating our RNAseq-based approach accurately measures the difference in OSN repertoires between strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ISH cell counts and RNAseq data for nine OR genes in both B6 and 129 strains, as shown in Figure 2K.

claim: 51 ORs contain 10 or more heterozygous SNPs in CAST genome sequence data, indicating additional alleles.
source: To assess this, we mined CAST genome sequence data (Keane et al., 2011) for heterozygous SNPs within annotated OR genes. We identified 51 ORs that contain 10 or more heterozygous SNPs, an indication of additional alleles.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of CAST genome sequence data from Keane et al., 2011.

claim: 30 novel or misassembled OR genes were identified in CAST using genome sequencing data.
source: Using genome sequencing data from these genes, we identified 30 novel or misassembled OR genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by de novo assembly and analysis of CAST genome sequencing reads.

claim: Only 12 of 634 OR genes lose their DE status after accounting for new OR alleles in CAST, and 4 OR genes become DE.
source: Only 12 of 634 OR genes lose their DE status, and 4 OR genes now become DE (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by re-analysis of differential expression after incorporating newly identified OR alleles, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The OSN repertoires cluster in two groups clearly defined by genetic background in the cross-fostering experiment.
source: We found that the OSN repertoires cluster in two groups, clearly defined by genetic background (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of RNAseq data from the cross-fostering experiment, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The correlation coefficient for any two B6 samples was on average 0.97 in the cross-fostering experiment.
source: The correlation coefficient for any two B6 samples was on average 0.97, with no significant difference between the environments (t-test, p=0.09).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RNAseq data from the cross-fostering experiment.

claim: The correlation for any B6 with a 129 sample had a mean of 0.89 in the cross-fostering experiment.
source: In contrast, the correlation for any B6 with a 129 sample had a mean of 0.89, which is significantly lower (t-test, p=3.8 × 10−12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RNAseq data from the cross-fostering experiment.

claim: 507 OR genes are differentially expressed between B6 and 129 mice when grouped by strain in the cross-fostering experiment.
source: Five hundred and seven OR genes, among 5475 other genes are DE between these mice when grouped by strain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from the cross-fostering experiment, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only two genes show differences in expression according to odor environment in the cross-fostering experiment, both of which encode ORs (Olfr875 and Olfr491).
source: In striking contrast, across the whole transcriptome we find only mRNA from two genes that show differences in expression according to odor environment, both of which encode ORs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis testing for environmental effects in the cross-fostering experiment, as shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 1,198 (95.9%) OSN subtypes are present in newborn pups across a dynamic range of abundance.
source: We identify the presence of 1,198 (95.9%) OSN subtypes across a dynamic range of abundance (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis of WOM from newborn B6 pups, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pseudogenized ORs are represented in OSNs with a very similar distribution to functional OR genes.
source: These are represented in OSNs with a very similar distribution to functional OR genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis of 134 annotated OR pseudogenes in B6 adult WOM, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 36.3% of the OSN subtypes that express identical ORs are differentially represented between 129 and B6.
source: Moreover, we analyzed the OR genes that encode identical protein-coding sequences between different strains. 36.3% of the OSN subtypes that express identical ORs are differentially represented between 129 and B6.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of OR genes with identical coding sequences but different expression levels between strains.

claim: 44.8% of OSN subtypes that express identical ORs are differentially represented between CAST and B6.
source: 44.8% are differentially represented between CAST and B6.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of OR genes with identical coding sequences but different expression levels between strains.

claim: Homozygous Olfr2 > Olfr1507 animals have 47 fold more Olfr2-expressing OSNs compared to controls.
source: Homozygous Olfr2 > Olfr1507 animals have 47 fold more Olfr2-expressing OSNs compared to controls, and is the highest subtype in these animals (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis of the Olfr2>Olfr1507 mouse line compared to wild-type controls, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 118 OSN subtypes show significant differences in the Olfr2 > Olfr1507 animals compared to controls, with over 90% having fold-changes < 2.
source: DE analysis of OR genes supports the striking reciprocal differences in Olfr1507 and Olfr2-expressing OSNs in the Olfr2 > Olfr1507 animals, but we also find 118 other OSN subtypes with significant, albeit comparatively subtle, differences (over 90% have fold-changes < 2) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from Olfr2>Olfr1507 mice, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Differentially represented OSN subtypes express OR genes with significantly greater amounts of variation in their coding sequence, whole transcript and regions of 300 bp or 1 kb upstream of the transcription start site for both 129 and CAST genomes.
source: We find that differentially represented OSN subtypes express OR genes with significantly greater amounts of variation in their coding sequence, whole transcript and regions of 300 bp or 1 kb upstream of the transcription start site, for both the 129 and CAST genomes (Mann-Whitney one tail, p<0.02 for 129 and p<0.0002 for CAST; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SNPs and indels in OR gene regions, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the CAST genome, 58 and 310 putative OR promoters have gains or losses of O/E and HD-binding sites respectively, compared to the B6 genome.
source: In the CAST genome, 58 and 310 putative OR promoters have gains or losses of O/E and HD-binding sites respectively, compared to the B6 genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of transcription factor binding sites in OR promoters.

claim: Only 12 and 46 OR promoters show differences in the number of O/E and HD-binding sites, respectively, when comparing the 129 and B6 genomes.
source: In contrast, only 12 and 46 OR promoters show differences in the number of O/E and HD-binding sites, respectively, when comparing the 129 and B6 genomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of transcription factor binding sites in OR promoters.

claim: 840 OSN subtypes (67.2%) expressed OR mRNAs that could be distinguished at the allelic level within F1 mice.
source: Within F1 mice, 840 OSN subtypes (67.2%) expressed OR mRNAs that could be distinguished at the allelic level.
evidence: This claim is supported by allele-specific RNAseq analysis of B6 x CAST F1 hybrids.

claim: The ratios between B6 and CAST OSN subtype abundance (F0) strongly correlate with the ratios between alleles in the F1 hybrids at approximately 1:1 (concordance correlation coefficient = 0.86).
source: The ratios between B6 and CAST OSN subtype abundance (F0) strongly correlate with the ratios between alleles in the F1 hybrids at approximately 1:1 (concordance correlation coefficient (ccc) = 0.86; Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by allele-specific expression analysis in F1 hybrids, as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: After correcting for technical noise, the F1 allelic expression data has a concordance correlation coefficient of 0.92.
source: The corrected data has a stronger correlation (ccc = 0.92) and the best fit of this data matches 1:1 concordance (Cb = 0.999).
evidence: This claim is supported by noise-corrected analysis of F1 allelic expression data, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 36 OR genes have significantly different mRNA levels (FDR < 5%) after 24 weeks of acute odor exposure to a mix of four odorants.
source: DE analysis reveals 36 OR genes with significantly different mRNA levels (FDR < 5%), with similar numbers more or less abundant in the exposed animals (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from mice exposed to odor mixture for 24 weeks, as shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: All seven tested OR genes with the biggest fold-changes in mRNA level have statistically significantly different expression from controls (t-test, FDR < 5%) after 24 weeks of acute odor exposure.
source: The results indicate that all the tested genes have mRNA levels that are statistically significantly different from controls (t-test, FDR < 5%) and the direction of the expression changes are concordant with the RNAseq data (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR validation of seven OR genes in a larger cohort, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After 1 week of acute odor exposure, none of the seven tested OR genes showed significant differences from controls.
source: After 1 week of treatment, none showed significant differences from controls, which is expected since young pups do not drink from the odorized water bottle.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR analysis at different time points, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After 4 weeks of acute odor exposure, three of the seven tested OR genes are differentially expressed from controls.
source: After 4 weeks, three of the OR genes are DE from controls, and at 10 weeks, five out of the seven receptors are DE (t-test, FDR < 5%; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR analysis at different time points, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After 10 weeks of acute odor exposure, five out of the seven tested OR genes are differentially expressed from controls.
source: After 4 weeks, three of the OR genes are DE from controls, and at 10 weeks, five out of the seven receptors are DE (t-test, FDR < 5%; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR analysis at different time points, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After 4 weeks of acute odor exposure followed by 6 weeks of recovery, none of the seven tested OR genes are differentially expressed from controls.
source: In these mice, none of the OR genes are DE from controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR analysis after recovery period, as shown in Figure 5D.

claim: None of the seven tested OR genes are differentially expressed after 24 weeks of chronic odor exposure.
source: None of the same seven OR genes are DE after 24 weeks, nor are any consistently dysregulated during the course of the exposure experiment (t-test, FDR < 5%; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR analysis of chronic odor exposure paradigm, as shown in Figure 5E.

claim: 43 OR genes are significantly differentially expressed (FDR < 5%) in at least one condition after 10 weeks of exposure to (R)-carvone, heptanal, or their combination.
source: We next carried out a transcriptome-wide analysis by RNAseq, finding 43 OR genes significantly DE in at least one of the conditions (FDR < 5%) of which 32 (74.4%) are upregulated in the odor-stimulated animals (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from mice exposed to individual odorants or their combination, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 32 out of 43 (74.4%) differentially expressed OR genes are upregulated in odor-stimulated animals after 10 weeks of exposure.
source: We next carried out a transcriptome-wide analysis by RNAseq, finding 43 OR genes significantly DE in at least one of the conditions (FDR < 5%) of which 32 (74.4%) are upregulated in the odor-stimulated animals (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Exposure to (R)-carvone resulted in a change in mRNA expression of 15 OR genes after 10 weeks.
source: Exposure to (R)-carvone or heptanal resulted in a change in mRNA expression of 15 and 20 OR genes, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from mice exposed to (R)-carvone, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Exposure to heptanal resulted in a change in mRNA expression of 20 OR genes after 10 weeks.
source: Exposure to (R)-carvone or heptanal resulted in a change in mRNA expression of 15 and 20 OR genes, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from mice exposed to heptanal, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Only one OR mRNA (Olfr538) is significantly upregulated in both (R)-carvone and heptanal exposure groups.
source: These sets of receptors are almost completely independent, with only one OR mRNA significantly upregulated in both groups (Olfr538; Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of differentially expressed OR genes, as shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Animals exposed to both (R)-carvone and heptanal simultaneously showed significant changes in mRNA levels for 24 OR genes.
source: The animals that were exposed to both odorants simultaneously showed significant changes in mRNA levels for 24 OR genes, 15 of which are shared with the individually exposed groups (hypergeometric test, p=1.87 × 10−19).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNAseq data from mice exposed to both odorants, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 15 out of 24 OR genes that are differentially expressed in animals exposed to both odorants are shared with the individually exposed groups (hypergeometric test, p=1.87 × 10−19).
source: The animals that were exposed to both odorants simultaneously showed significant changes in mRNA levels for 24 OR genes, 15 of which are shared with the individually exposed groups (hypergeometric test, p=1.87 × 10−19).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing differentially expressed OR genes across exposure conditions.

claim: Almost 40% of the ORs that show significant changes when exposed to all four odorants are also significantly altered in one or more of the groups exposed to (R)-carvone, heptanal or their combination.
source: Almost 40% of the ORs that show significant changes when exposed to all four odorants (Figure 5B) are also significantly altered in one or more of the groups exposed to (R)-carvone, heptanal or their combination.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of differentially expressed OR genes across different odor exposure experiments.

claim: Olfr538 displayed a dose-dependent response to (R)-carvone in vitro.
source: Half of the DE ORs we tested were responsive in vitro (Figure 6E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B): for example, Olfr538 displayed a dose-dependent response to (R)-carvone (Figure 6E) and Olfr524 was responsive to heptanal (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data showing dose-response curve for Olfr538 with (R)-carvone, as shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Olfr524 was responsive to heptanal in vitro.
source: Half of the DE ORs we tested were responsive in vitro (Figure 6E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B): for example, Olfr538 displayed a dose-dependent response to (R)-carvone (Figure 6E) and Olfr524 was responsive to heptanal (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data showing dose-response curve for Olfr524 with heptanal, as shown in Figure 6F.

claim: 12 and 210 OR mRNAs were significantly enriched (FDR < 5%) upon exposure to 1% and 100% heptanal, respectively, in the pS6-IP experiment.
source: Twelve and 210 OR mRNAs were significantly enriched (FDR < 5%) upon exposure to 1% and 100% heptanal, respectively, compared to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by pS6-immunoprecipitation and RNAseq analysis after heptanal exposure.

claim: Over half (11 out of 20) of the differentially expressed ORs after 10-week acute exposure to heptanal are also differentially expressed in the pS6+ cells (hypergeometric test, p=0.0001).
source: Over half of the DE ORs after 10-week acute exposure to heptanal (Figure 6B) are also DE in the pS6+ cells (11 out of 20; Figure 6G), which is significantly more than expected by chance (hypergeometric test, p=0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of differentially expressed OR genes between long-term acute exposure and pS6-IP experiments, as shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The mouse genome codes for over a thousand functional OR genes.
source: The mouse genome codes for over a thousand functional OR genes, but each mature OSN expresses only one abundantly, in a monoallelic fashion (Hanchate et al., 2015; Saraiva et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2015; Chess et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on OR gene expression.

claim: Each mature OSN expresses only one OR gene abundantly, in a monoallelic fashion.
source: The mouse genome codes for over a thousand functional OR genes, but each mature OSN expresses only one abundantly, in a monoallelic fashion (Hanchate et al., 2015; Saraiva et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2015; Chess et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hanchate et al., 2015; Saraiva et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2015; Chess et al., 1994.

claim: The MOE contains approximately 10 million OSNs within the nose of a mouse.
source: This results in a highly heterogeneous repertoire of approximately 10 million OSNs (Kawagishi et al., 2014) within the nose of a mouse, stratified into more than a thousand functionally distinct subpopulations, each one characterized by the particular OR it expresses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kawagishi et al., 2014.

claim: Reproducible differences in abundance have been observed between OSNs expressing different ORs.
source: For the scarce data available (<10% of the full repertoire) reproducible differences in abundance have been observed between OSNs expressing different ORs (Bressel et al., 2016; Fuss et al., 2007; Khan et al., 2011; Young et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bressel et al., 2016; Fuss et al., 2007; Khan et al., 2011; Young et al., 2003.

claim: Most promoters of OR genes contain binding sites for Olf1/Ebf1 (O/E) and homeodomain (HD) transcription factors.
source: Most promoters of OR genes contain binding sites for Olf1/Ebf1 (O/E) and homeodomain (HD) transcription factors (Young et al., 2011), and these are involved in determining the probability with which the OR genes are chosen for expression (Rothman et al., 2005; Vassalli et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Young et al., 2011; Rothman et al., 2005; Vassalli et al., 2011.

claim: O/E and HD transcription factors are involved in determining the probability with which OR genes are chosen for expression.
source: Most promoters of OR genes contain binding sites for Olf1/Ebf1 (O/E) and homeodomain (HD) transcription factors (Young et al., 2011), and these are involved in determining the probability with which the OR genes are chosen for expression (Rothman et al., 2005; Vassalli et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rothman et al., 2005; Vassalli et al., 2011.

claim: Enhancer elements regulate the gene choice frequencies of nearby, but not distally located, ORs.
source: Enhancer elements also regulate the gene choice frequencies of nearby, but not distally located, ORs (Khan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Khan et al., 2011.

claim: Activation extends a sensory neuron's life-span.
source: Indeed activation extends a sensory neuron's life-span (Santoro and Dulac, 2012), suggesting that persistent exposure to particular odorants may, over time, increase the relative proportions of the OSNs responsive to them.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Santoro and Dulac, 2012.

claim: Some OSN subtypes reportedly increase in number in response to odor activation, but others do not.
source: Some OSN subtypes do reportedly increase in number in response to odor activation, but others do not (Cadiou et al., 2014; Cavallin et al., 2010; Watt et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cadiou et al., 2014; Cavallin et al., 2010; Watt et al., 2004.

claim: The main olfactory epithelium is an essential component of the olfactory sensory system.
source: The main olfactory epithelium (MOE) is an essential component of the olfactory sensory system.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the olfactory system.

claim: ORs are the proteins that bind odorants.
source: It contains olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) that express olfactory receptors (ORs), the proteins that bind odorants (Buck and Axel, 1991; Zhao et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buck and Axel, 1991; Zhao et al., 1998.

claim: The monogenic nature of OR expression serves as a molecular barcode for OSN subtype identity.
source: The monogenic nature of OR expression serves as a molecular barcode for OSN subtype identity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the established fact that each OSN expresses one OR gene.

claim: 3.6% or less of the OSN subtypes contribute to 25% of the overall neuronal content of the WOM.
source: In fact, 3.6% or less of the OSN subtypes contribute to 25% of the overall neuronal content of the WOM.
evidence: This claim is inferred from analysis of the OSN distribution data showing unequal representation.

claim: Proximity to the H element, a cluster-specific enhancer, increases the frequency in which an OR is represented within the OSN population.
source: Proximity to the H element, a cluster-specific enhancer, increases the frequency in which an OR is represented within the OSN population (Khan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Khan et al., 2011.

claim: Higher levels of OR transcription per cell may result in more OSNs expressing that receptor due to increased success in a post-selection refinement process.
source: Recently, it has been proposed that higher levels of OR transcription per cell may result in more OSNs expressing that receptor due to increased success in a post-selection refinement process (Abdus-Saboor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Abdus-Saboor et al., 2016.

claim: The MOE is continually replacing its OSN pool.
source: The MOE is continually replacing its OSN pool and the birth of every neuron presents an opportunity to shape the proportion of different subpopulations.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the regenerative capacity of the olfactory epithelium.

claim: Relative OSN abundances could be altered by regulating the lifespan of each OSN subtype.
source: It is also possible that relative OSN abundances could be altered by regulating the lifespan of each OSN subtype.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: The probability of choice of OR genes linked to the H element are regulated in cis.
source: Moreover, through analysis of F1 hybrids, we confirmed the finding that the probability of choice of OR genes linked to the H element are regulated in cis (Fuss et al., 2007), and extended this to over 800 additional OR genes distributed throughout the genome that show little to no evidence in support of trans-acting regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fuss et al., 2007 and by the F1 hybrid data in this study.

claim: Trans interactions of multiple enhancers may stabilize or maintain OR singularity after choice has been instructed in cis.
source: These trans interactions may, however, stabilize or maintain OR singularity after choice has been instructed in cis, and thus could also be necessary for the stereotypic representation of OSNs in a fixed genetic background.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: The transposition of Olfr2 OSNs to a different olfactory zone may alter the dynamics and spatial organization of the glomeruli in the olfactory bulb.
source: One plausible hypothesis is that the transposition of Olfr2 OSNs to a different olfactory zone alters the dynamics and spatial organization of the glomeruli in the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain observed data.

claim: Stabilizing trans interactions could be affected by the OR gene swap, resulting in slightly altered repertoires for some OSN subtypes.
source: Alternatively, stabilizing trans interactions could be affected by the OR gene swap, resulting in slightly altered repertoires for some OSN subtypes.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative hypothesis to explain observed data.

claim: The difference between acute and chronic odor exposure effects is a result of olfactory adaptation in the presence of continuous stimulation.
source: We propose that this difference is a result of olfactory adaptation in the presence of continuous stimulation.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The lengthy timeframe for odor-mediated differences to emerge is consistent with modulation of OSN lifespan.
source: The lengthy timeframe for odor-mediated differences to emerge is consistent with modulation of OSN lifespan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics observed in the odor exposure experiments.

claim: Odor-activity could promote OR expression stabilization or singularity.
source: It is mechanistically unlikely that odor-activity could influence the probability of OR gene choice, but it could promote OR expression stabilization or singularity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Humans differ in up to a third of their OR alleles by functional variation.
source: Humans differ in up to a third of their OR alleles by functional variation (Mainland et al., 2014), which contributes to an individually unique sense of smell (Secundo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mainland et al., 2014 and Secundo et al., 2015.

claim: Segregating OR alleles have been functionally linked to perceptual differences of their odor ligands, by altering intensity, valence or detection threshold.
source: Segregating OR alleles have been functionally linked to perceptual differences of their odor ligands, by altering intensity, valence or detection threshold (Jaeger et al., 2013; Keller et al., 2007; Mainland et al., 2014; McRae et al., 2013; Menashe et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on OR genetic variation and perception.

claim: OR coding genetic variants explain only a small proportion of the observed phenotypic variance in most cases.
source: However, in most cases, these OR coding genetic variants explain only a small proportion of the observed phenotypic variance (reviewed in Logan [2014]), suggesting that other factors contribute to individual differences in perception.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review by Logan, 2014.

claim: Increasing the number of a particular OSN subtype in a mouse nose increases olfactory sensitivity to its ligand.
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated that increasing the number of a particular OSN subtype in a mouse nose increases olfactory sensitivity to its ligand (D'Hulst et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to D'Hulst et al., 2016.

claim: An array-based study of OR expression in 26 humans found unequal expression of ORs within and between individual noses.
source: Although it remains to be determined whether human OSN repertoires are as variable as the mice reported here, an array-based study of OR expression in 26 humans found unequal expression of ORs within and between individual noses (Verbeurgt et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Verbeurgt et al., 2014.

claim: A systematic survey of olfactory perception in humans found high levels of individual variability in reporting the intensity of some odors but not others.
source: Moreover, a recent systematic survey of olfactory perception in humans found high levels of individual variability in reporting the intensity of some odors (for example, benzenethiol and 3-pentanone) but not others (Keller and Vosshall, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Keller and Vosshall, 2016.

claim: A non-coding variant within an OR cluster associated with insensitivity to 2-heptanone has been shown to be dominant to the sensitive allele.
source: Further, a non-coding variant within an OR cluster associated with insensitivity to 2-heptanone has been shown to be dominant to the sensitive allele (McRae et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McRae et al., 2013.

claim: Many odorants activate multiple OSN subtypes.
source: On the other hand, because many odorants activate multiple OSN subtypes (Malnic et al., 1999), a differential representation of one subtype may have a limited influence on the overall perception of its odor.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Malnic et al., 1999.
